name: Zero-sum thinking
statement: People judge that one party's gain must come at another's expense, including in situations where nothing fixes the total available.
meaning: Two claims travel under this name and they are measured with different instruments. The perceptual claim is that people misread particular situations, inferring that a resource is capped when it is not. The attitudinal claim is that people differ in how readily they agree with statements such as 'if someone gets richer it means that someone else gets poorer', and that this agreement can be scored and correlated with politics, trust and income. Shai Davidai and Stephanie Tepper, reviewing the field for Nature Reviews Psychology, separate a general mindset about how social relations work from domain-specific beliefs about trade, immigration, race, gender and status. They note that the second approach has produced work in contexts as far apart as college grades, corporate profits, LGBTQ rights and romantic relationships. Almost all of the large-scale evidence concerns agreement with statements rather than misperception of a situation.

origin.note: The paper is "Zero-Sum Bias: Perceived Competition Despite Unlimited Resources", article 191 in the journal's first volume, published on 5 November 2010. Its 28 references contain no work by George Foster and its text never uses the phrase 'image of limited good'; the link between zero-sum thinking and Foster's 1965 account of peasant societies is drawn later, by Davidai and Tepper and by Chinoy and colleagues, who open their paper with it. The belief-scale tradition runs separately. Joanna Różycka-Tran, Paweł Boski and Bogdan Wojciszke published the 37-nation study in 2015, and the 43-nation paper's reference list gives an earlier Polish-language scale paper by Różycka and Wojciszke in Studia Psychologiczne in 2010.

evidence: Meegan ran three experiments at the University of Guelph, whose regulations bar instructors from grading to a fixed distribution. Participants saw the grades of the first 19 presenters in a 20-student course and predicted the 20th. In Experiment 1, 556 undergraduates saw either a negatively skewed distribution or a symmetrical one, 278 in each condition. The skew pushed predictions down, χ²(4) = 50.30, p < 0.001, with D predictions more frequent, χ²(1) = 30.56, p < 0.001, and A predictions less frequent, χ²(1) = 5.63, p < 0.05. Experiment 2 reversed the skew for 308 students, 154 per condition, and its overall test was significant, χ²(4) = 13.77, p < 0.01. No matching rise in high-grade predictions followed. Its one significant cell ran the way a normative reading predicts, with D predictions more frequent in the positively skewed condition, χ²(1) = 7.20, p < 0.01. Experiment 3 gave half of 368 students the text of the grading policy, χ²(4) = 18.28, p < 0.005, which cut D predictions, χ²(1) = 5.77, p < 0.05, and F predictions, χ²(1) = 9.00, p < 0.005. Samuel Johnson, Jiewen Zhang and Frank Keil found the same error in ordinary trade. They recruited 100 people and analysed 86, dropping 14 who missed more than a third of the comprehension questions. Shown 12 everyday transactions, 94.2% said at least one party was left worse off somewhere, and 88.4% called at least one transaction zero-sum or negative-sum. Buyers were judged worse off about five times as often as sellers, 2.53 transactions of 8 against 0.49, t(85) = 7.55, p < 0.001, d = 1.11. Sahil Chinoy, Nathan Nunn, Sandra Sequeira and Stefanie Stantcheva surveyed roughly 20,400 US residents in seven waves between October 2020 and July 2023, scoring agreement with four statements about ethnic groups, citizenship, trade and income classes. Those four correlated between 0.29 and 0.57 and loaded on one component with an eigenvalue of 2.30.

replication.headline: The eight-item belief scale holds its one-factor shape in all of 36 countries, while agreement with logically equivalent zero-sum statements changes when the two halves are swapped.
replication.detail: Joanna Różycka-Tran, Paweł Jurek, Michał Olech, Jarosław Piotrowski and Magdalena Żemojtel-Piotrowska fitted the Belief in a Zero-Sum Game scale separately in student samples from 36 countries, 9,907 people, and report a one-factor structure in all of them, with configural and metric invariance across countries. Only the abstract of that paper was read here; the publisher refused the full text. The detailed fit statistics on this page come from a companion study by Różycka-Tran, Guido Alessandri, Jurek and Olech, which pooled 11,368 respondents from 43 countries in two waves of 5,158 and 6,210. The single-level one-factor model fitted, χ²(20) = 1084.69, CFI = .959, RMSEA = .068. Standardised loadings ran from .36 to .79 within countries and .72 to .99 between them. Strong isomorphism, which forces equal loadings across levels and zero country-level residuals, failed, CFI = .428, RMSEA = .093. Freeing those residuals restored fit, CFI = .921, RMSEA = .037, so the scale means roughly the same thing at both levels only once country-specific item bias is allowed for. About 8% of the variance in the latent belief sat between countries. Of five country indicators tested, only gross national income per head and individualism correlated negatively with it. None of this is independent replication. The 43-nation paper names its first wave as the data of the 2015 study that introduced the scale and its second wave as the data of the 36-country study, and all three carry Różycka-Tran as first author. Michael Smithson and Yiyun Shou tested the measure from the other side. A zero-sum statement has the form 'the more X for A, the less Y for B', and its four permutations should be endorsed equally by anyone who believes it. Their Study 1 drew 508 completed surveys from American adults, 395 of them usable, and five of six statements showed an effect of which permutation was offered, all χ²(3) > 21.0, p < 0.001. The exception was a statement about investment, χ²(3) = 3.6, p = 0.312. Study 2 repeated the test on rating scales with usable samples of 405 Americans, 426 Britons and 452 Indians, and Study 3 on a seven-point scale with 498 Americans, 494 Britons, 503 Indians and 496 Chinese. Most asymmetries held across the samples, including for a statement about cloudy weather and sunshine that really is zero-sum. Almos Molnar and Steven Sloman report five studies in Cognition in which political framing switches the bias on and off, with Democrats finding less effective solutions to a problem framed as corporate tax cuts and Republicans finding less effective solutions to the same problem framed as pro-immigration policy. Its full text was not obtained, so no sample size or test statistic from it appears here. Searches of Crossref, PubMed, OpenAlex and the open web on 17 August 2026, including the 97 works Semantic Scholar records as citing Meegan, located no repetition of his grade-prediction experiments.

study.cite: Różycka-Tran, J., Jurek, P., Olech, M., Piotrowski, J., & Żemojtel-Piotrowska, M. (2019). Measurement invariance of the Belief in a Zero-Sum Game scale across 36 countries. International Journal of Psychology, 54(3), 406-413.

limits: The evidence is overwhelmingly correlational, and the review of the field says so plainly: Davidai and Tepper write that the difficulty of manipulating zero-sum beliefs has led many researchers to rely on correlational and cross-sectional research designs. The Chinoy paper is a survey. Its links between zero-sum scores and support for redistribution, affirmative action and immigration restriction survive controls for demographics, party and seven other beliefs, among them whether luck beats effort, moral universalism, generalised trust and trust in government. Its ancestry results are of the same kind. Greater mobility from parents to respondent went with a lower zero-sum score, b = -0.0220, SE 0.0016, in 13,131 respondents, on an index running from 0 to 1 with a mean of 0.529 and a standard deviation of 0.222. Reporting an enslaved ancestor went with a higher score, b = 0.0834, SE 0.0054, in the full sample of 20,263, where the index has a mean of 0.514 and a standard deviation of 0.211. Experiments exist, and their outcomes are usually judgements or hypothetical choices. Patricia Andrews-Fearon and Shai Davidai recruited 300 people and analysed 297 after one attention check, telling them that a new employer either ranked staff against each other or judged each against a fixed criterion. The ranking description raised zero-sum ratings, d = 1.47, 95% CI [1.21, 1.73], and led participants to pick more dominance books from a list of eight, d = .75, 95% CI [.51, .98]. The outcome there was a book choice rather than a job or a payment. Hemant Kakkar and Niro Sivanathan do measure behaviour. Their preregistered Study 3 recruited 501 people and analysed 413, and telling participants their group leader was dominant rather than prestigious raised zero-sum mindset, F(1, 411) = 20.12, p < .001, d = .44, and cut the characters they transcribed to help another member, b = -.35, SE .005, p < .001 in a Poisson regression. The same study carries a null: zero-sum mindset did not predict the yes-or-no choice to help, p > .10, so their proposed mediation failed on that measure. Kevin Wei and Fan Yang cut the other way. In two preregistered studies, US adults and children aged 4 to 9 did not treat love, trust, popularity or leadership as zero-sum, and rated all four less zero-sum than material goods such as stickers. Meegan's own paper concedes two rival readings of his result: Guelph students rarely see many top grades awarded in practice, so wariness may be reasonable, and they may have learned to treat school as one more contest for limited career opportunities. His participants were undergraduates at one university. Sirola and Pitesa's 2017 study of economic downturns and workplace helping was not retrieved. The publisher's page and the green copy in Singapore Management University's repository both refused the request on 17 August 2026, and Crossref carries no abstract for it, so no figure from it appears here. The 2015 paper that introduced the belief scale was not retrieved either, after attempts at the publisher, at ResearchGate and through Semantic Scholar on the same date. Its sample of 6,138 across 37 countries is quoted from the 43-nation paper's description of it, and that paper separately describes the same study as supplying 5,158 respondents from 30 countries.
misreadings: The idea is usually attached to the political right. Chinoy and colleagues found the opposite alignment on three of their four items, with Democrats more zero-sum about ethnic groups, trade and income, and Republicans more zero-sum about citizenship. Republicans in their sample were less zero-sum on average. The same paper reports the pattern outside the United States, using the World Values Survey item put to about 192,000 people in 72 countries. Conditional on country and survey wave, a higher zero-sum score goes with a more left-leaning self-placement, slope -0.47, SE 0.02, across 188,317 observations. That single item correlates with their own four-question index at ρ = 0.18 among the 8,801 respondents asked both. Davidai and Ongis make a different claim from six studies with 3,223 participants. Conservatives rated challenges to the status quo as zero-sum and liberals rated its preservation as zero-sum, so the sign of the correlation follows the direction of the policy rather than the party. Meegan's bias is also quoted as if it ran both ways. It did not. Many high grades already given made low predictions more likely, while many low grades did not make high predictions more likely, which is why he calls the heuristic unidirectional. Agreeing that the rich get rich at the expense of the poor is not the same act as misreading an uncapped situation as capped, and a person can do either without doing the other. In some settings the zero-sum reading is correct, and a scale score cannot tell the two cases apart. The lump of labour fallacy at entry 456 is a narrower proposition about one market, and it is kept separate here.

sources.text: Meegan, D. V. (2010). Zero-sum bias: Perceived competition despite unlimited resources. Frontiers in Psychology, 1, 191. Full text read at Frontiers. Source for the three experiments, the condition sizes and every chi-square on this page, and checked for the absence of Foster and of the phrase 'image of limited good'.

Foster, G. M. (1965). Peasant society and the image of limited good. American Anthropologist, 67(2), 293-315. Crossref confirms author, title, journal, volume, issue, pages and year. Named by Davidai and Tepper and by Chinoy and colleagues as the antecedent; not cited by Meegan.

Różycka-Tran, J., Boski, P., & Wojciszke, B. (2015). Belief in a zero-sum game as a social axiom: A 37-nation study. Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology, 46(4), 525-548. Only the abstract at Crossref was read. The publisher and ResearchGate both refused the full text on 17 August 2026 and Semantic Scholar records no open copy. The abstract states neither a sample size nor a country count.

Różycka-Tran, J., Jurek, P., Olech, M., Piotrowski, J., & Żemojtel-Piotrowska, M. (2019). Measurement invariance of the Belief in a Zero-Sum Game scale across 36 countries. International Journal of Psychology, 54(3), 406-413. Only the abstract at Crossref was read; it is the source for the 36 countries, the 9,907 respondents, the one-factor structure in all countries and the configural and metric invariance.

Różycka-Tran, J., Alessandri, G., Jurek, P., & Olech, M. (2018). A test of construct isomorphism of the Belief in a Zero-Sum Game scale: A multilevel 43-nation study. PLOS ONE, 13(9), e0203196. Manuscript XML read direct from PLOS. Source for the fit statistics, the loadings, the 8% between-country variance, the country indicators, the description of the 37-nation sample as 6,138 and the identification of the two waves with the 2015 and 2019 papers. Its reference list also carries the 2010 Polish-language scale paper.

Smithson, M., & Shou, Y. (2016). Asymmetries in responses to attitude statements: The example of "zero-sum" beliefs. Frontiers in Psychology, 7, 984. PDF read direct from Frontiers, which carries the chi-square symbols and degrees of freedom that the HTML rendering drops. Source for the permutation effects, the 508 completed and 395 usable cases in Study 1, and the four national samples.

Johnson, S. G. B., Zhang, J., & Keil, F. C. (2022). Win-win denial: The psychological underpinnings of zero-sum thinking. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 151(2), 455-474. Read twice from two independent copies, the author's accepted manuscript in the Warwick repository and a copy of the published article, which agree on 100 recruited, 14 excluded, 94.2%, 88.4%, t(85) = 7.55 and d = 1.11.

Chinoy, S., Nunn, N., Sequeira, S., & Stantcheva, S. (2026). Zero-sum thinking and the roots of US political differences. American Economic Review, 116(3), 1052-1096. Figures here were read off the published article, hosted by the authors' Social Economics Lab. Source for the 20,400 respondents, the seven waves, the eigenvalue of 2.30, the 0.29 to 0.57 correlations, Table 2, Table 6, the seven belief controls and the World Values Survey figures.

Davidai, S., & Ongis, M. (2019). The politics of zero-sum thinking: The relationship between political ideology and the belief that life is a zero-sum game. Science Advances, 5(12), eaay3761. Full text read at PubMed Central; source for the six studies, the 3,223 participants and the status-quo reversal.

Andrews-Fearon, P., & Davidai, S. (2023). Is status a zero-sum game? Zero-sum beliefs increase people's preference for dominance but not prestige. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 152(2), 389-409. Full text read from a copy of the published article. Source for Study 5A, its 300 recruited and 297 analysed, the eight books, and both effect sizes with intervals.

Davidai, S., & Tepper, S. J. (2023). The psychology of zero-sum beliefs. Nature Reviews Psychology, 2(8), 472-482. Full text read from a copy of the published review. Source for the general and domain-specific split, the list of domains, the Foster attribution and the sentence about correlational and cross-sectional designs.

Kakkar, H., & Sivanathan, N. (2022). The impact of leader dominance on employees' zero-sum mindset and helping behavior. Journal of Applied Psychology, 107(10), 1706-1724. Accepted manuscript read from the London Business School repository, and its abstract checked against PubMed. Source for Study 3, the 501 recruited and 413 analysed, the dominance manipulation, the Poisson coefficient on characters transcribed and the failed mediation on the binary helping measure.

Molnar, A. C., & Sloman, S. A. (2026). Zero-sum bias in politicized problem solving. Cognition, 270, 106408. Abstract read at PubMed. Named for its five studies and its framing result; the full text was refused by the publisher on 17 August 2026 and no figure from it appears here.

Wei, K., & Yang, F. (2025). Love doesn't run out: Children and adults do not view social resources as inherently zero-sum. Social Psychological and Personality Science, 16(8), 855-865. Abstract read at Crossref; source for the two preregistered studies and the finding that love, trust, popularity and leadership were rated less zero-sum than material goods.

Sirola, N., & Pitesa, M. (2017). Economic downturns undermine workplace helping by promoting a zero-sum construal of success. Academy of Management Journal, 60(4), 1339-1359. Crossref confirms authors, title, journal, volume, issue, pages and year and carries no abstract. Neither the publisher's page nor the repository copy at Singapore Management University could be opened on 17 August 2026, so nothing from it is quoted.
